node.label: Annette Gordon-Reed
node.date_label: Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings (1997) · The Hemingses of Monticello (2008) · “Most Blessed of the Patriarchs,” with Peter S. Onuf (2016) · On Juneteenth (2021)
node.description: In Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings (1997), Annette Gordon-Reed argued that evidence of the Jefferson–Hemings relationship had been denied a fair hearing, pointing to inconsistencies in noted scholars' evaluations and their exclusion of evidence concerning the Hemings family. The Hemingses of Monticello (2008) reconstructed an enslaved family’s relationships to make its members historical subjects in their own right. Edmund S. Morgan and Marie Morgan praised its fresh perspective; Jill Lepore admired the work while questioning inferences from human nature. With Peter S. Onuf, Gordon-Reed examined Jefferson’s understanding of himself as patriarch in “Most Blessed of the Patriarchs” (2016). Gordon S. Wood praised its insights but criticized its uneven joint voice and its account of the Jefferson–Hamilton conflict. Her writing also answers criticism of biography as a form of history writing (2014) and combines Texas history with memoir in On Juneteenth (2021).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings: An American Controversy (1997; paperback 1998); The Hemingses of Monticello: An American Family (2008); Writing Early American Lives as Biography (2014); “Most Blessed of the Patriarchs”: Thomas Jefferson and the Empire of the Imagination (2016), with Peter S. Onuf; On Juneteenth (2021).
node.scope_note: Book arguments are supported by publisher descriptions, the author’s interviews and named contemporary reviewers. The 1997, 2008, 2016 and 2021 books were not read in full. Selected 2014 essay passages and the 2019 Taylor review were read directly. Andrew Johnson was read only in a publisher introduction excerpt; other listed chapters and the teaching video remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In their review of The Hemingses of Monticello (2008), Edmund S. Morgan and Marie Morgan praise Gordon-Reed’s reconstruction for bringing fresh perspectives to a Jefferson long scrutinized by biographers.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Review opening, second substantive paragraph, beginning The Hemingses of Monticello: “fresh perspectives.” Joint reception, not Morgan alone; no claim of direct influence on the book. Monograph unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Gordon-Reed and Peter S. Onuf’s “Most Blessed of the Patriarchs” (2016), Wood praises its insights but criticizes its uneven joint voice and its treatment of the Jefferson–Hamilton conflict as too personal.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher review, paragraphs beginning Although the two authors and But this claim: “a single voice” and “great political and social interests.” Criticism concerns the coauthored book; does not establish which author wrote a passage. Book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In President Tom’s Cabin (2008), Lepore praises The Hemingses of Monticello (2008) while questioning its reliance on analogies and assumptions about human nature.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paragraph beginning Gordon-Reed rested her case: “could do with more mortar.” Specific caution about inference, alongside praise; not rejection of the paternity case. Books unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Hemingses of Monticello (2008) makes enslaved people historical subjects by reconstructing family and social relationships marginalized by accounts centred on Jefferson.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2017 interview, answer following Did you know after your first book: “tell their story” and “web of relationships.” Own retrospective explanation of the book’s purpose; complete book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings (1997) argues that evidence of the Jefferson–Hemings relationship had been denied a fair hearing, pointing to inconsistencies in noted scholars' evaluations of the evidence and their exclusion of evidence from the Hemings family.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher summary, paragraphs 1–3: “fair hearing”; 2017 interview, answer beginning Instead I thought about teaching: “not proof” but “certainly evidence.” Original book body unread. The claim concerns evaluating evidence, not laboratory proof.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Keeping Their Stories Alive (2026), Gordon-Reed explains how historical and legal scholarship guides her work on Harvard’s public account of its ties to slavery and the memory of enslaved people.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Q&A, answers to Why is the work and Council expertise: “educational mission” and “support of the law.” Current advisory practice, not a claim that an institutional project is complete.

proposed_edges.relationship: In his 2008 review of Annette Gordon-Reed’s The Hemingses of Monticello (2008), Eric Foner praised her research and reconstruction of the wider family but criticized her interpretation of the Jefferson–Hemings relationship as an enduring romance, arguing that other readings of the limited evidence were equally plausible.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on Foner’s own website. Its praise of research and family reconstruction does not remove its explicit criticism of the romance interpretation. This records Foner’s assessment, not an independent finding about the relationship. The book itself was not read for this task.
